definition: Rife means abundant, widespread, especially with something undesirable.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word rife. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know rife should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: By the third week of the heat wave, the marina was rife with complaints about the algae smell.
Common stops short of rife — a common problem turns up here and there, while a rife one meets you at every corner.
Rampant goes further than rife — what is rife saturates a place; what is rampant is still multiplying, out of anyone's control.

Riddled means shot through with holes or flaws — a hull riddled with leaks, a report riddled with errors — the emphasis on damage at every point. Rife views the same saturation from the other side: the trouble itself is what is abundant, present everywhere at once.

Teeming means swarming with life or activity — a teeming reef, a teeming market — and it leans neutral or even admiring. Rife tilts hard toward trouble: a place is rife with errors, mold, or corruption, never happily rife with kindness.

Rife has spent a thousand years in English without producing a single everyday relative — no verb, no noun, no adjective cousins. What it kept instead is a habit: it works after the noun it describes, usually with 'with.' Rumors are rife; corruption is rife with something. You will almost never meet 'a rife rumor.'
Rife means abundant, widespread, especially with something undesirable.
The inspector's report made the old dormitory sound like a hazard catalogue: wiring rife with splices, stairwells rife with loose treads, and a basement he declined to certify at all.
Rife is abundance gone wrong — you rarely hear of a town rife with kindness.
The word does its best work in the pattern rife with, flagging a place or system shot through with trouble: errors, mold, corruption.

Rife is a reporter's word and a predicate one: markets are rife with fraud; you would not write 'a rife market.' For neutral abundance use full of or teeming with; keep rife for infestations — of error, vermin, or corruption — and keep it after the noun.

Twenty years ago the town's volunteer historical society launched a wiki, hoping residents would document every house on the register.
Enthusiasm outran verification.
By the time a retired archivist audited the site, it was rife with errors: invented architects, dates copied from the wrong county, a founding legend traced to a joke in an 1890s newspaper column.
The archivist's tally was sobering -- of four hundred entries, fewer than sixty survived without correction.
She resisted deleting the wiki, arguing that the mistakes themselves were now part of the town's story.
Instead, each corrected page keeps its old error visible, struck through, beside the documented fact.
